analytic.title: A Novel Hardware-Software Codesign of Network Protocol Stacks on a SoC platform

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: In this paper, we propose a novel hardware-software codesign technique of network protocol stacks on a SoC (System on Chip) platform for providing the QoS (Quality of Service) functionality. We address that the codesign should guarantee the real-time performance of periodic packets and minimize the average response time of aperiodic packets in order to provide the QoS functionality. We present the following three mechanisms to resolve this issue: 1) task decomposition technique of a network protocol suite into hardware and software tasks, 2) a communication channel between heterogeneous tasks, 3) finegrained and coarse-grained real-time processing simultaneously for application-specific real-time requirements. A case study based on experiments is conducted to illustrate the efficiency of the proposed technique by implementing it on the commercial SoC platform embedded with the Altera's Excalibur EPXA4 including ARM922T core and 400K gates of programmable logic.

div.head: INTRODUCTION
div.p: Recently, several mechanisms implementing network protocol cores into hardware component based on hardwaresoftware codesign in a commercial SoC (System on Chip) have been studied in order to improve the quality of networking services [1][2][3]. The applications as video and audio which have specific real-time requirements are rarely conducted in the existing proposed methods. We address the issue of the network protocol stack guaranteeing the real-time performance of periodic packets and minimizing the average response time of aperiodic packets for providing the QoS (Quality of Service) functionality. We present the following three mechanisms to resolve this issue with hardware-software codesign. First, we present a task decomposition technique to implement the network protocol suite into hardware and software tasks. The network protocols implemented in hardware can be faster than the network protocols implemented in software because they avoid sequential processing of individual functions and perform multiple computation activities at the same time through parallel processing [4]. Specifically, the major reasons for building the hardware tasks are to satisfy performance requirements. Additionally, the task decomposition technique can improve co-design productivity by supporting the modularity and reuse of complex network protocol cores, thus the task decomposition technique enable a higher level of abstraction in architectural modeling of future network protocol specifications. Second, we implement a communication channel based on message queues between the heterogeneous tasks in order to synchronize the activities of the decomposed tasks. The problem to be considered is specification and synthesis of real-time inter-task communication interface among software-to-software, software-to-hardware, and hardware-to-hardware tasks. Third, we also consider the functionality required for real-time processing of application tasks and protocol functions. What it is need to be studied is the question of how to design a data frame unit with real-time features, to provide the inter-task communication channel which concurrently carries messages between software and hardware elements, and to explain how both fine-grained and coarse-grained real-time processing. This paper is organized as follows. Section II investigates the related work that motivates us to work on the task decomposition technique, the communication channel between heterogeneous tasks, and the real-time processing with messages. Section III presents the dynamic real-time networking platform developed in this research work. Section IV analyzes theoretically the performance of the proposed technique. In Section V, the proposed technique is evaluated in terms of the performance of hardware tasks, the deadline-miss ratio of periodic packets, the response time of aperiodic packets, the deadline-miss ratio of periodic tasks, and the processor utilization. Section VI concludes this paper.

div.head: II. MOTIVATION
div.p: We discuss the existing approaches to the sub-problems of hardware-software co-design for embedded real-time network/multimedia systems in terms of system partitioning, RTOS (Real-Time Operating System) containing real-time scheduling, synchronization between hardware and software tasks, hardware-software communication interface, applicationspecific QoS and high performance considering TOE (Traffic Offload Engine). References [5][6][7][8][9] have attempted to present a hardware-software partitioning technique for a mixed system. References [5][6] consider the partition problem on the feasibility of hardware-software implementation and the satisfaction of non-real timing constraints. Reference [7] provides an excellent review of partitioning problems in terms of the following approaches: partitioning toward a preexisting or fixed hardware platform and traditional VLSI (Very Large Scale Integration) partitioning. Especially, reference [8] presents a flexible method that focuses on physical and architectural constraints imposed on dynamically reconfigurable architecture by partial reconfiguration feature. However, related work addressed in [7][8] ignores the issues of real-time scheduling and QoS constraints for given applicationspecific requirements. Recent work presented in [9] considers a flexible multiprocessor SoC platform that supports high-speed hardware-assisted messaging, context-switching, and scheduling. However, it does not consider real-time scheduling incorporating the concept of task and message transmission deadline but only high-priority, fair-sharing based on a roundrobin scheme, and best-effort scheduling. Reference [10] defines the QoS and cost model for communications in SoC and classifies SoC inter-module communication traffic into four classes of service: signaling for inter-module control signals, real-time for delay-constrained bit streams, short data access modeling, and block-transfer for large data bursts. However, they do not address more details of specifying QoS and real-time technique for task and packet scheduling. The work presented in [1-3][11-12] discusses an architectural solution for protocol layer on-chip implementation and the high performance issue in existing protocols such as the TCP/IP protocol suite. In terms of the architectural solution of protocol layer on-chip implementation, the IEEE802.11a MAC (Medium Access Control) layer on-chip implementation [1] and the TCP/IP protocol layer implementation [2][3] have been presented. As discussed in [11][12], one central question of TCP/IP high performance has been whether it would be more appropriate to implement TCP in host CPU software, or in the network interface system. The latter approach is usually called TOE. Especially, reference [12] addresses that TOE per se is neither of much overall benefit nor free from significant costs and risks. However it propose that TOE in the service of very specific goals might actually be useful. The HASIS (Hardware Software Interface Synthesis) communication channel supporting message scheduling in reference [13] is based on weighted fair queues for avoiding starvation. Reference [14] proposes a hybrid scheduling scheme based on non-preemptive EDF (Earliest Deadline First) algorithm in order to meet message deadlines and maximize network utilization. We implement and evaluate the scheduling schemes presented by reference [13][14] to compare the performances of providing QoS functionality with our proposed technique. In the research work presented in this paper, we attempt to reconsider these features, which have been reviewed so far in this section at different concepts, and then we succeed in building a SoC platform for real-time embedded network/multimedia systems that can resolve a decomposing problem of implementing any network protocol suite into real-time application-specific and reconfigurable hardware/software tasks. Note that the mixed systems based on heterogeneous S/W (SoftWare) and H/W (HardWare) tasks execute complex functionality and strong interactions among tasks.

div.head: III. REAL-TIME NETWORKING SOC PLATFORM
div.p: The hardware-software codesign of SoC platform proposed in this paper is shown in Figure 1. The implementation of the SoC Platform were carried out using the Excalibur EPXA4 Device [15] with the LAN91C111 10/100 Ethernet chip [16] produced by SMSC corporation. The RTOS running kernel on the SoC platform is implemented in this paper by modifying and improving the version of uC/OS [17].

The first consideration of designing the SoC platform supporting multitasking is the principal division of system functions and tasks -the architecture of RTOS kernel, communication protocol tasks, and runtime environment. In the proposed SoC platform, the RTOS kernel provides the smallest possible set of services and resources on which the remaining services required can be built. This basic set of services includes task management, time management, and service of task synchronization (i.e. binary/counting semaphore). Thus one of main jobs in this research work is to decompose each of all system functions including network protocols into the corresponding task. The task decomposition technique can support the coarse-grained real-time processing by partitioning all significant system functions into tasks and keeping the deadline of tasks through a real-time scheduler. We take advantage of the RM (Rate Monotonic) scheme with giving the highest priority to the task with the highest rate of execution [18]. In order to provide real-time data exchange enabling bidirectional communication between S/W and H/W tasks, we design a special unified inter-communication interface, which is called the ITC technique incorporating the RTHC 2 (Real-Time Heterogeneous task Communication Channel). All S/W and H/W tasks attached to different AHBs (ARM Advanced High-performance Bus) have the same ITC interface. Thus S/W and H/W tasks can be easily, dynamically loaded. Additionally, the data generated from all services provided by S/W and H/W tasks are exchanged over the ITC using the HCM (Heterogeneous task Communication Message). A HCM is referred to as a piece of data frame unit and is scheduled by HCM-scheduler for a level of support for fine-grained but realtime communications among S/W and H/W tasks in remote hardware logic. Namely, the proposed SoC platform has no notion of other bothersome arbiter operations built into it but new system services and network protocol layers can be dynamically loaded and accessed by a real-time message-based mechanism. As for real-time processing schedulers provided by the RTHC 2 , PITnDST (Period Inheritance to the corresponding Task period and Distributing Slack Time to the aperiodic HCM) proposed in this paper. Also the HASIS scheduler and the EDF scheduler proposed in the existing researches are exploited in experiments. The maximum degree of openness and dynamic heterogeneous reconfiguration can be achieved with this approach that has been described so far.

The PITnDST scheduling mechanism is composed of the PIT module and the DST module. Each module schedules different target, but makes up for the weak points of each other. The PIT module is the mechanism that inherits the period property of the periodic HCM to the period property of the task which would process the periodic HCM in order to guarantee the deadline of the periodic HCM. The DST module is the mechanism that schedules an aperiodic HCM to execute first as far as all periodic tasks and all periodic HCM are schedulable in order to minimize the response time of the aperiodic HCM. The operations of PIT module are as follows: if the total utilization of the set of periodic tasks and periodic HCMs is no greater than 1 at the release time , task τ 4 has higher priority than task τ 1 . After periodic task τ 4 preempts task τ 3 which is the aperiodic task, task τ 4 is completed at 27.5 and task τ 3 runs. Unfortunately this results HCM η 1 missing its deadline. Second, let us assume that the PIT scheduler proposed in this paper is used in the transactions. The periodic property and the value of period of periodic HCM η 1 are inherited to task τ 3 after other tasks turn out to be feasibly scheduled by the PIT scheduler. Then η 1 frame is forwarded to task τ 3 . Task τ 1 and task τ 4 simultaneously arrive at time 20. Since

, task τ 3 has higher priority than task τ 4 and task τ 1 . Task τ 3 is successfully completed at time 25 and also HCM η 1 keeps its deadline successfully. This example shows why we propose the PIT scheduler for a level of support for fine-grained but realtime communications among S/W and H/W tasks.

div.head: IV. ANALYSIS OF RESPONSE TIME OF APERIODIC HCM
div.p: The real-time processing of S/W and H/W tasks running on the SoC platform is handled by a real-time task scheduler. Besides, as soft real-time applications running on the SoC platform, such as multimedia or videoconferencing, where HCMs containing voice and audio packet are being transmitted through the RTHC 2 , the need to deliver HCMs in a timely fashion is equally obvious. Excessive delays in message delivery can significantly degrade the QoS provided. That's why we consider real-time features such as the proposed PITnDST scheduler and real-time properties included in the HCM as illustrated in Figure 2 when HCMs are exchanged between S/W and H/W tasks through the ITC incorporating the RTHC 2 . The HCM schedulers presented in this paper basically attempt to keep the deadline of periodic HCMs while the task schedulers do so for given a set of tasks at the same time. Consequently, we need to analyze the response time of aperiodic HCMs processed by HCM schedulers in terms of high performance measurement of systems if all HCMs are feasibly scheduled by a given task and HCM schedulers. Let us now set out to find out how more efficient the proposed PITnDST scheduler is than the FIFO (First-In First-Out) and the PIT schedulers running over RM task schedulers in terms of the response time of an aperiodic HCM. Table I describes the average execution times of other TCP/IP network protocol tasks. The performance of CHK-TX and CHK-RX tasks in hardware is superior to that of corresponding CHK-TX and CHK-RX tasks in software and remains almost equal even if the packet size is increased to 1450 bytes. These two hardware tasks exploit parallelism increasing their execution speeds while activating the buffer transfer mode supported by the AHB to enhance data transfer rate as fast as 32bytes per a single clock edge. In all hardware tasks connecting to the AHB interface, all timing is referenced to a single clock edge to control all of their operations. Thus, each of all hardware tasks yields better performance than corresponding software task.

Figure 6 shows the average deadline miss ratios of periodic packets from the application layer to the physical layer when seven kinds of TCP/IP protocol implementation are evaluated. 1) Original-TCP/IP is the original version of well-known uIP [23]. 2) Decomposed-TCP/IP: the TCP/IP which is decomposed into the proposed heterogeneous task per protocol model, but does not use the proposed RTHC. 3) Decomposed-TCP/IP with RTHC-FIFO is the TCP/IP which is decomposed into the proposed heterogeneous task per protocol model with the RTHC, and uses the FIFO scheduling scheme in RTHC. 4) Decomposed-TCP/IP with RTHC-HASIS is identical with the Decomposed-TCP/IP with RTHC-FIFO except for using the scheduling scheme proposed by [13]. 5) Decomposed-TCP/IP with RTHC-EDF is identical with the Decomposed-TCP/IP with RTHC-FIFO except for using the scheduling scheme proposed by [14]. 6) Decomposed-TCP/IP with RTHC-PIT is identical with the Decomposed-TCP/IP with RTHC-FIFO except for using the scheduling scheme with the PIT module except the DST module. 7) Decomposed-TCP/IP with RTHC-PITnDST is identical with the Decomposed-TCP/IP with RTHC-FIFO except for using the PITnDST scheduling scheme proposed in this paper. The real-time performance of the scheduling schemes like the Decomposed-TCP/IP with RTHC-EDF, the Decomposed-TCP/IP with RTHC-PIT, and the Decomposed-TCP/IP with RTHC-PITnDST is better than others because they consider the deadline of packets.

Figure 7 shows the average response times of aperiodic packets from the application layer to the physical layer. In case of the Decomposed-TCP/IP with RTHC-FIFO, the Decomposed-TCP/IP with RTHC-PIT, and the Decomposed-TCP/IP with RTHC-PITnDST, theoretical outcomes derived from (4), (5), and (6) are compared with outcomes generated by experiments. Additionally, we confirm that the proposed Decomposed-TCP/IP with RTHC-PITnDST scheme yields lower average response time of the aperiodic packets than the Decomposed-TCP/IP with RTHC-PIT and the others. Figure 8 shows the average deadline miss ratio of periodic tasks. All of the TCP/IP models have similar values of average deadline miss ratio. In case of ρ = 0.9, each of average deadline miss ratio of the Original-TCP/IP, the Decomposed-TCP/IP, the Decomposed-TCP/IP with RTHC-FIFO, the Decomposed-TCP/IP with RTHC-HASIS, the Decomposed-TCP/IP with RTHC-EDF, the Decomposed-TCP/IP with RTHC-PIT and the Decomposed-TCP/IP with RTHC-PITnDST are 5.79%, 4.32%, 4.81%, 5.38%, 5.63%, 5.79%, and 5.81% respectively. The main issue of this paper is to resolve the hardwaresoftware co-design problem of implementing network protocols in the SoC architecture which considers the application-specific real-time requirements for given multimedia/networking applications. We also address the issue of implementing any protocol network protocol suite into reconfigurable hardware and software tasks. Currently, the multimedia applications of the TCP/IP protocol stack vary in a wide range of devices. Thus after we apply the nearly full specifications of TCP/IP protocol suite into our SoC platform, we verify and validate the performance of SoC platform incorporating the ITC technique incorporating the RTHC 2 . Experimental results indicate that the proposed technique yields efficient performance in terms of deadline miss ratio of periodic packets, average response time of aperiodic packets, and processor utilization of all mixed S/W and H/W tasks.
